A '''boxology''' is a representation of an organized structure as a [[graph theory|graph]] of labeled nodes ("[[rectangle|boxes]]") and connections between them (as [[line (geometry)|line]]s or [[arrow (symbol)|arrows]]).  The concept is useful because many problems in systems design are reducible to modular "black boxes" and connections or flow channels between them.  The term is somewhat tongue-in-cheek <ref>{{cite book |last= Raymond |first=Eric |title=The New Hacker's Dictionary|url=https://archive.org/stream/jarg422/jarg422.txt|date=1996|isbn=978-0262680929|publisher=The MIT Press}}</ref> and refers to the generic nature of diagrams containing labelled nodes and (sometimes directed) paths between them.<ref>
Daniel Dennett.
"Things about Things".
Chapter 9, p. 138 in:
Joao Branquinho, editor.
[https://books.google.com/books?id=Q-Je_1uJWigC "The Foundations of Cognitive Science"].
2001.
quote: "controversy has raged about the right way to draw the connecting boxes that compose the flow charts -- the "boxology" -- ..."
</ref>

The archetypical example of a boxology is a corporate [[organizational chart|"org chart"]], which describes lines of control through the corporation.  Other boxologies include programming [[flow chart]]s,<ref>
Richard Menary, editor.
[https://books.google.com/books?id=gf4z86DNKzsC "Radical Enactivism"].
p. 34.
quote: "flowchart boxology, of the sort inspired by a traditional input-output functionalism."
</ref><ref>
Terence Horgan; Terry Horgan; John Tienson.
[https://books.google.com/books?id=VaL5uioJo0gC "Connectionism and the Philosophy of Psychology"].
1996.
p. 22.
quote: "In terms of familiar flow-chart analyses ("boxology", as Cummins (1983) puts it), one adds a lower sublevel by adding more interconnected boxes ... either between existing boxes or within them."
</ref>
system-level [[circuit diagram]]s for designing large complex circuits, and even economic models.
[[Feynman diagrams]] are useful because they reduce the complicated [[mathematics]] of [[quantum mechanics]] to a simple boxology of particle interactions.

Depending on application, the boxes are optional; for example, the global [[carbon cycle]] is modeled as a boxology, but many figures explaining the model include only labels and directed connections.
